section.heading: 11.6. The Ratio and Root Tests
section.paragraph: One way to determine how quickly the terms of a series are decreasing (or increasing) is to calculate the ratios of consecutive terms. For a geometric series $$\sum ar^{n - 1}$$ we have $$\left| a_{n + 1}/a_{n} \middle| = \middle| r \right|$$ for all $$n$$ , and the series converges if $$\left| r \middle| < 1 \right.$$ . The Ratio Test tells us that for any series, if the ratios $$\left| a_{n + 1}/a_{n} \right|$$ approach a number less than $$1$$ as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , then the series converges. The proofs of both the Ratio Test and the Root Test involve comparing a series with a geometric series.
section.heading: The Ratio Test
section.paragraph: The following test is very useful in determining whether a given series is absolutely convergent.

list.item: (i) If $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left. \middle| \frac{a_{n + 1}}{a_{n}} \right| = L < 1$$ , then the series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n}$$ is absolutely convergent (and therefore convergent).

(ii) If $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left. \middle| \frac{a_{n + 1}}{a_{n}} \right| = L > 1$$ or $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left. \middle| \frac{a_{n + 1}}{a_{n}} \right| = \infty$$ , then the series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n}$$ is divergent.

(iii) If $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left. \middle| \frac{a_{n + 1}}{a_{n}} \right| = 1$$ , the Ratio Test is inconclusive; that is, no conclusion can be drawn about the convergence or divergence of $$\sum a_{n}$$ .

(i) The idea is to compare the given series with a convergent geometric series. Since $$L < 1$$ , we can choose a number $$r$$ such that $$L < r < 1$$ . Since $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left| \frac{a_{n + 1}}{a_{n}} \right| = L$$ and $$L < r$$ the ratio $$\left| {a_{n + 1} \slash a_{n}} \right|$$ will eventually be less than $$r$$ ; that is, there exists an integer $$N$$ such that $$\left| \frac{a_{n + 1}}{a_{n}} \right| < r \text{whenever} n \geqslant N$$ or, equivalently, $$\left| a_{n + 1} \right| < \left| a_{n} \right|r \text{whenever} n \geqslant N$$ Putting $$n$$ successively equal to $$N,{N + 1},{N + 2,\ldots}$$ in (1), we obtain $$\begin{array}{l} \left| a_{N + 1} \middle| < \middle| a_{N} \middle| r \right. \\ \left| a_{N + 2} \middle| < \middle| a_{N + 1} \middle| r < \middle| a_{N} \middle| r^{2} \right. \\ \left| a_{N + 3} \middle| < \middle| a_{N + 2} \middle| r < \middle| a_{N} \middle| r^{3} \right. \end{array}$$ and, in general, $$\left| a_{N + k} \right| < \left| a_{N} \right|r^{k} {for all}k \geqslant 1$$ Now the series $$\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{\infty}\left| a_{N} \middle| \right.r^{k} = \left| a_{N} \right|r + \left| a_{N} \right|r^{2} + \left| a_{N} \right|r^{3} + \cdots$$ is convergent because it is a geometric series with $$0 < r < 1$$ . So the inequality (2), together with the Direct Comparison Test, shows that the series $$\sum\limits_{n = N + 1}^{\infty}\left| a_{n} \right| = {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{\infty}\left. \middle| a_{N + k} \right| = \left| a_{N + 1} \right| + \left| a_{N + 2} \right| + \left| a_{N + 3} \middle| + \cdots \right.}$$ is also convergent. It follows that the series $$\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty}\left| a_{n} \right|$$ is convergent. (Recall that a finite number of terms doesn’t affect convergence.) Therefore $$\sum a_{n}$$ is absolutely convergent.

(ii) If $$\left. \left| {a_{n + 1} \slash a_{n}} \right|\rightarrow L > 1 \right.$$ or $$\left. \left| {a_{n + 1} \slash a_{n}} \right|\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , then the ratio $$\left| {a_{n + 1} \slash a_{n}} \right|$$ will eventually be greater than $$1$$ ; that is, there exists an integer $$N$$ such that $$\left| \frac{a_{n + 1}}{a_{n}} \right| > 1 \text{whenever} n \geqslant N$$ This means that $$\left| a_{n + 1} \right| > \left| a_{n} \right|$$ whenever $$n \geqslant N$$ and so $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}a_{n} \neq 0$$ Therefore $$\sum a_{n}$$ diverges by the Test for Divergence.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Test the series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}{\left( {- 1} \right)^{n}\frac{n^{3}}{3^{n}}}$$ for absolute convergence.
Solution We use the Ratio Test with $$a_{n} = \left( {- 1} \right)^{n}n^{3} \slash 3^{n}:$$

$$\begin{array}{l} {\left. \left| \frac{a_{n + 1}}{a_{n}} \right| = \left| \frac{\frac{\left( {- 1} \right)^{n + 1}\left( {n + 1} \right)^{3}}{3^{n + 1}}}{\frac{{({- 1})}^{n}n^{3}}{3^{n}}} \right. \right| = \frac{{({n + 1})}^{n}}{3^{n + 1}} \cdot \frac{3^{n}}{n^{3}}} \\ \left. \phantom{\left| \frac{a_{n + 1}}{a_{n}} \right|} = \frac{1}{3}\left( \frac{n + 1}{n} \right)^{3} = \frac{1}{3}\left( {1 + \frac{1}{n}} \right)^{3}\rightarrow\frac{1}{3} < 1 \right. \end{array}$$
Thus, by the Ratio Test, the given series is absolutely convergent.

note.title: Estimating Sums
note.heading: Estimating Sums
note.paragraph: In the preceding three sections we used various methods for estimating the sum of a series—the method depended on which test was used to prove convergence. What about series for which the Ratio Test works? There are two possibilities: If the series happens to be an alternating series, as in Example 1, then it is best to use the methods of Section 11.5. If the terms are all positive, then use the special methods explained in Exercise 42.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Test the convergence of the series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{n^{n}}{n!}$$ .
Solution Since the terms $$a_{n} = n^{n} \slash n!$$ are positive, we don’t need the absolute value signs.

$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{a_{n + 1}}{a_{n}} = \frac{\left( {n + 1} \right)^{n + 1}}{\left( {n + 1} \right)!} \cdot \frac{n!}{n^{n}} = \frac{\left( {n + 1} \right)\left( {n + 1} \right)^{n}}{\left( {n + 1} \right)n!} \cdot \frac{n!}{n^{n}}} \\ \left. \phantom{\frac{a_{n + 1}}{a_{n}}} = \left( \frac{n + 1}{n} \right)^{n} = \left( {1 + \frac{1}{n}} \right)^{n}\rightarrow e {as}n\rightarrow\infty \right. \end{array}$$
(see Equation 3.6.6). Since $$e > 1$$ , the given series is divergent by the Ratio Test.

section.paragraph: Note Although the Ratio Test works in Example 2, an easier method is to use the Test for Divergence. Since
it follows that $$a_{n}$$ does not approach $$0$$ as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ . Therefore the given series is divergent by the Test for Divergence.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Part (iii) of the Ratio Test says that if $$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left| {a_{n + 1} \slash a_{n}} \right| = 1$$ , then the test gives no information. For instance, let’s apply the Ratio Test to each of the following series:
$$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}}$$
In the first series $$a_{n} = 1/n$$ and
$$\left. \left| \frac{a_{n + 1}}{a_{n}} \right| = \frac{1/(n + 1)}{1/n} = \frac{n}{(n + 1)}\rightarrow 1 {as}n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$
In the second series $$a_{n} = 1/n^{2}$$ and
$$\left. \left| \frac{a_{n + 1}}{a_{n}} \right| = \frac{1/\left( {n + 1} \right)^{2}}{1/n^{2}} = \left( \frac{n}{n + 1} \right)^{2}\rightarrow 1 {as}n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$

In both cases the Ratio Test fails to determine whether the series converges or diverges, so we must try another test. Here the first series is the harmonic series, which we know diverges; the second series is a $$p$$ -series with $$p > 1$$ , so it converges.
The Ratio Test is usually conclusive if the $$n$$ th term of the series contains an exponential or a factorial, as in Examples 1 and 2. The test will always fail for $$p$$ -series, as in Example 3.

section.heading: The Root Test
section.paragraph: The following test is convenient to apply when $$n$$ th powers occur. Its proof is similar to the proof of the Ratio Test and is left as Exercise 45.

list.item: (i) If $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sqrt[n]{\left| a_{n} \right|} = L < 1$$ , then the series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n}$$ is absolutely convergent (and therefore convergent).

(ii) If $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sqrt[n]{\left| a_{n} \right|} = L > 1$$ or $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sqrt[n]{\left| a_{n} \right|} = \infty$$ , then the series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n}$$ is divergent.
(iii) If $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sqrt[n]{\left| a_{n} \right|} = 1$$ , the Root Test is inconclusive.

section.paragraph: If $$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sqrt[n]{\left| a_{n} \right|^{}} = 1$$ , then part (iii) of the Root Test says that the test gives no information. The series $$\sum a_{n}$$ could converge or diverge. (If $$L = 1$$ in the Ratio Test, don’t try the Root Test because $$L$$ will again be $$1$$ . And if $$L = 1$$ in the Root Test, don’t try the Ratio Test because it will fail too.)

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Test the convergence of the series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\left( \frac{2n + 3}{3n + 2} \right)^{n}$$ .
Solution

$$\begin{array}{rll} a_{n} & = & \left( \frac{2n + 3}{3n + 2} \right)^{n} \\ \sqrt[n]{\left| a_{n} \right|^{}} & = & \left. \frac{2n + 3}{3n + 2} = \frac{2 + \frac{3}{n}}{3 + \frac{2}{n}}\rightarrow\frac{2}{3} < 1 \right. \end{array}$$
Thus the given series is absolutely convergent (and therefore convergent) by the Root Test.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Determine whether the series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\left( \frac{n + 1}{n} \right)^{n}$$ converges or diverges.
Solution Here it seems natural to apply the Root Test:
$$\left. \sqrt[n]{\left| a_{n} \right|^{}} = \frac{n + 1}{n}\rightarrow 1 {as}n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$
Since this limit is $$1$$ , the Root Test is inconclusive. However, using Equation 3.6.6 we see that
$$\left. a_{n} = \left( \frac{n}{n + 1} \right)^{n} = \frac{1}{\left( \frac{n + 1}{n} \right)^{n}}\rightarrow\frac{1}{e} {as}n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$
Since this limit is different from zero, the series diverges by the Test for Divergence.

section.paragraph: Example 5 serves as a reminder that when testing a series for convergence or divergence it is often helpful to apply the Test for Divergence before attempting other tests.
